masthead_title: Friday's selloff pushed the S&P 500 into a correction, and the bond market agreed with it.
regime_line: Friday's 3.70% S&P 500 drop — this year's second-largest, after Nov. 5 — left the index 11.62% below its October record, a confirmed correction, while Treasurys rallied across every maturity into territory the 30-year last revisited, briefly, in June 2007.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — nothing resolves today, two still open

CL-0072 (Wednesday's hawkish FOMC minutes marking a genuine new leg of the dollar's climb, not a one-day reaction) — not resolved today. Its deadline is today, but today's own close isn't in yet at this pre-market hour, so the test finishes in tomorrow's brief. Two of its three sessions are in: Thursday's 103.90 cleared the 103.86 confirm line, Friday's 103.81 didn't — though it stayed nowhere near the 103.49 refute level either.

CL-0073 (Thursday's broad four-way agreement across rates, credit, the dollar, and breadth marking a genuine extension of the selloff, not a one-day echo of Anthropic's debut volatility) — not due until 2026-11-25. One of its three sessions is in: Friday's S&P 500 close of 6,910.39 is already below the 7,175.83 confirm reference, and HY and IG OAS both remain flagged — leaning toward confirming the extension, but two sessions remain.
story_html:
Friday extended this month's AI-led unwind into a second, sharper leg. The S&P 500 fell 3.70% to 6,910.39, the Nasdaq-100 fell 5.28%, and the index closed 11.62% below its October 6 record — a confirmed correction. Coverage (amgreatness.com, “AI Sell-Off Drags Dow, S&P 500 Into Correction as Nasdaq's Gains for the Year Vanish”) framed the week as the S&P 500's worst percentage loss since April 2025, tying it to the same AI/chip-stock doubts that opened this selloff on Nov. 5. No weekend news of substance turned up in today's search — this Monday edition is built from Friday's own session plus today's calendar, nothing more invented to fill the gap.

This system's own pull confirms the broad framing but sharpens where the damage actually landed. Small caps (Russell 2000, −2.76%) and the equal-weight S&P (RSP, −1.98%, now itself flagged for the first time in weeks) both fell less than the cap-weighted indexes — real pain, but not as concentrated in a handful of giants as Friday's headline number suggests. Chips absorbed far more than their share: SMH fell 10.60%, and the Technology sector ETF (XLK, −7.27%) diverged from the S&P (−3.64%) by 3.63 percentage points, the day's only sector move of that size — every other sector ETF (staples, health care, energy, utilities, real estate, financials) actually outperformed the index (Movers, below). That argues for “a severe but concentrated tech/AI unwind” over “a market-wide panic,” even on a day this bad. Treasurys rallied across every tenor — the 10-year eased to 4.92%, the 30-year to 5.31%, a level that, before this run, was last touched in June 2007 (History, below) — and credit stayed wide (HY and IG OAS both still flagged). The dollar, by contrast, barely moved (DXY −0.09%): three of this system's four hierarchy votes leaned risk-off together, but the fourth just sat still, a reminder that Friday's agreement has to be read fresh rather than assumed to match Thursday's cleaner four-way case.
dashboard_interp_html:
Every Treasury tenor eased again — still consistent with money moving into safety, not a Fed story. The 3-month bill fell 2bp to 4.32% but is up over the past five sessions (z +1.68, flagged; 53rd percentile since the early 1980s but the 72nd of the last 30 years). The 2-year fell 13bp to 4.63% (z +0.75, below the flag line; 50th percentile over the full ~50-year record but the 79th of the last 30 years, † a 29-point gap). The 10-year fell 12bp to 4.92% (z +0.48, below the flag line; 46th/82nd %ile, †). The 30-year fell 9bp to 5.31% (z +0.38; 46th/81st %ile, † — today's lead History-check fact, below: before this run, this level was last touched, briefly, in June 2007). The curve barely moved at the long end (2s10s +1bp to 29bp, z −1.21) but flattened at the front (3m10y −10bp to 60bp, z −1.61, flagged). Why this matters: a bond is a loan, and its yield is what the borrower pays to borrow for that long — Treasury yields falling across every maturity on a day stocks fell hard is the clearest single piece of evidence that Friday was a genuine flight-to-safety move, not just money rotating out of one sector into another.

Credit stayed wide, the dollar barely moved, and gold and copper fell anyway — without the dollar doing the work this time. HY OAS — the extra yield investors demand to lend to junk-rated companies over safe Treasurys — widened 5bp to 3.52% (dated Thursday 11-19, the usual one-session lag; z +2.37, flagged; 88th percentile of its own ~3-year record, marked * since this live series has no multi-decade history, §4F). IG OAS, the investment-grade equivalent, rose 1bp to 0.94% (also dated Thursday; z +2.40, flagged; 76th percentile of its own ~3-year record, marked *). The dollar (DXY) was essentially flat at 103.81 (−0.09%; z +2.41, this run's largest Tier 1 flag on a running basis; 75th percentile over the full ~55-year dollar record and the 84th of the last 30 years). Gold fell 4.62% to $3,515.40 (z −3.57, its third straight flagged session) and copper fell 2.63% (z −4.40) — both falling hard, but this time not because the dollar did it (Concept, below): with DXY barely moved, Friday's drop in two assets with very different reputations (one a traditional safe haven, one an industrial-growth bellwether) reads as a broader liquidation that didn't spare either, not a repeat of last week's dollar-driven mechanism. Why this matters: when the usual explanation for a move stops fitting the day's own numbers, that's worth noticing before repeating it to a client as if nothing changed.
history_html:
Today's deepest echo is the 30-year Treasury, now at 5.31%, first reaching this level Aug. 17 and there on 41 of the 67 sessions since — not every session. Before this run, the last time was June 2007, and only briefly (one session). This run's own high, 5.67% on Oct. 7, was last matched in July 2001. The two lenses disagree: 81st percentile of the last 30 years, just 46th of the full 50-year record — unusual lately, unremarkable across the full sweep, since the longer record folds in the double-digit 1970s/’80s (every reading in the 1980s was at or above today's 5.31%). Against June 2007, the level is close (5.35% then vs. 5.31% now), but policy wasn't: fed funds sat at 5.25% then, near a cyclical peak before the 2007-09 crisis, versus SOFR's 3.91% now.

Second: the 10-year TIPS real yield (2.88%, Thursday) sits at the 99.5th percentile of its own 24-year record, there on 15 of the 37 sessions since Sep. 28. Before this run, last reached November 2008, inside the 2007-09 crisis, and only briefly. The Cleveland Fed's longer model, back to 1982, reads far milder: the 80th percentile of the last 30 years, just the 54th since 1982 — TIPS alone are too short a history to call this extreme on their own.

Third: Friday's 3.70% S&P 500 drop is a move of a size that comes about 2 days a year over the last 30 years; it's the second this year, and the last bigger one was Nov. 5. Client-ready: two readings — the 30-year Treasury and 10-year real yield — are revisiting 2007-09 crisis-era levels, but the policy backdrop differs; the echo is in the level, not the cause.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically, plus the top-50 megacaps; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) or a sector ETF diverging ≥1.5pp from SPX, never by seeming interesting. 116 name candidates qualified Friday (up from 58 Thursday) and 7 sector ETFs cleared the divergence bar (up from 0 Thursday). Earnings/guidance reactions are prioritized per §5; Intuit reported Thursday evening and is covered first. Nvidia is covered for its direct Tier 3 relevance despite no company-specific Friday news found. Also qualifying, left out under the cap: LITE (−13.94%), MU (−13.89%), AMD (−13.25%), COHR (−12.90%), P (−12.75%), STX (−12.35%), AVGO (−12.19%), WDC (−12.02%) — not individually researched today given the cap; none asserted to lack a catalyst, simply not checked.

Intuit (INTU) −12.77% (270.44, from 310.02) — what happened: fiscal Q1 FY2027 results, released after Thursday's close, the clearest earnings/guidance-driven decline on this screen. Stated reason: per Simply Wall St (“Intuit (INTU) Stock Price Drops After Q1 Earnings Guidance Cut”) and Investing.com's earnings analysis, Intuit beat on the quarter — non-GAAP EPS $2.91 vs. roughly $2.70 expected, revenue $4.35 billion vs. roughly $4.31 billion expected, up 12% year over year — but Q2 FY2027 revenue guidance of $4.93–$4.95 billion came in below consensus and full-year guidance was trimmed slightly; both outlets tied the drop specifically to the guidance trim, not the beat. Read-through: the same “a beat today can still be a sell on tomorrow's guide” pattern this curriculum has already taught twice this cycle — a demand signal that was fine, undercut by a forward number that wasn't what the market had priced; useful for any client holding software broadly, not a software-sector-wide read on its own.

Bloom Energy (BE) −15.30% (142.39, from 168.11) — what happened: the day's single largest decline on this screen, with no earnings, filing, or company announcement behind it. Stated reason: per Trefis (“What Moved Bloom Energy Stock?”), the drop reflects investors broadly dumping AI-data-center-infrastructure-linked stocks that day, not anything specific to Bloom — Trefis notes the decline ran more than twice its own sub-industry's median move. Read-through: explicitly idiosyncratic to the group, not the company — directly Tier 3-relevant as a clean read on how hard sentiment toward AI-adjacent power/infrastructure names turned Friday, independent of any one name's fundamentals.

Nvidia (NVDA) −14.01% (125.53, from 145.98) — what happened: fell alongside the broader semiconductor/AI-hardware complex — MU, AMD, AVGO, LITE, COHR, STX, WDC, and dozens more all down double digits the same session (Movers list, above). Stated reason: no new Nvidia-specific news surfaced in today's search; its own Q3 FY2027 beat, $150 billion buyback, and above-consensus outlook were Tuesday's story, and CL-0071 already refuted the idea that print would turn the complex around (resolved 2026-11-20). Friday's drop reads as that same retreat continuing, not a fresh catalyst. Read-through: directly Tier 3-relevant; four sessions after interim CEO Colette Kress's first earnings call, the complex is falling further, not stabilizing — the live evidence against CL-0071's hoped-for turning point.
chart_of_day_why: The S&P 500 carries this run's single largest |z| move of any series today at −4.80, ahead of SPY (−4.70), the Nasdaq-100 (−4.66), and copper (−4.40) — a reflection of Friday's 3.70% drop, the broadest and most decisive single-session move behind this week's selloff, and the obvious anchor for today's chart regardless of which single stock or sector moved most.
tier3_html:
Daily read: SMH underperformed SPY by 6.96 percentage points Friday (−10.60% vs. −3.64%) — the widest gap of any session since the broad complex-wide rout earlier this month (Movers/Story, above), and far wider than Thursday's narrower 0.66-point gap. Friday's selloff hit the chip/AI-hardware complex disproportionately hard even as the rest of the market fell too: XLK's −7.27% and SMH's −10.60% both dwarfed the S&P's own −3.70%, consistent with a concentrated-but-severe tech/AI unwind rather than an undifferentiated panic.

Weekly issuance/spread note: no fresh, dated hyperscaler-issuance or vendor-financing news surfaced in today's search beyond what's already in recent briefs; this week's own HY/IG OAS prints (Dashboard, above), both still flagged into Friday, remain the live reading on AI-adjacent credit appetite. The next weekly structured half-page (§5 Tier 3) runs Friday 2026-11-27, a holiday-shortened week.
calendar_note_html:
Today: no high-impact scheduled release. Flash Manufacturing PMI (cons. 54.5, prior 56.0) and Flash Services PMI (cons. 55.6, prior 57.9), both 9:45am ET, are the session's only medium-impact prints; the Fed's Williams speaks at 4:00pm ET, low-impact on the calendar. Markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving with a half-day Friday, so Wednesday's releases — Core PCE and Preliminary Q3 GDP, both high-impact, 8:30am ET — are effectively this week's last full data read before the holiday, and also the day CL-0073 (Flags, below) comes due.

Why this matters to the current regime: after Friday's rout, a soft PMI print would read as the real economy starting to catch up to what markets already priced in; a strong one would complicate the growth-scare framing building in credit and the dollar. Today's own calendar is light enough that the more decisive test is still two sessions away.
concept_title: Same assets falling, different reason — gold and copper's drop wasn't the dollar's doing this time
concept_html:
Segment 7 taught that gold and copper are dollar-priced, so when both fall together it's often the dollar doing the work, not an independent vote on growth or fear — Thursday's brief used exactly that mechanism to explain gold's drop. Today looks the same on the surface: gold fell 4.62% and copper fell 2.63%, both flagged for a third straight session. But the mechanism isn't the same. The dollar barely moved Friday (DXY −0.09%, essentially flat) while Treasurys rallied and credit stayed wide — the textbook flight-to-safety signature. Gold, the asset that's supposed to benefit most from exactly that signature, fell instead.

The habit worth building: check the mechanism fresh each session rather than assuming yesterday's explanation still applies because the price action looks similar. With the dollar not doing the work Friday, the honest read is a broader liquidation that didn't spare gold or copper either — not a repeat of last week's dollar-driven story, even though the two charts look alike.
client_translation: Gold fell again Friday, but don't assume it's the same "strong dollar" story as before — the dollar barely moved that day, which means something broader was pressuring even the traditional safe havens, worth knowing before a client asks why gold isn't protecting them this week.
client_lens_html:
“Did you see what happened Friday? Are we in a crash?” The S&P 500 is now in a confirmed correction (11.62% below its October record), but it's still up 0.95% for the year — worth saying plainly, since “correction” and “the year is a loss” aren't the same thing yet. We've got two live tests running (CL-0072, CL-0073; Claims/Flags, above) on whether this extends or echoes.

“Is this just a chip/AI problem, or is everything falling?” Both, in different degrees. Every major index fell Friday, but chips and the broader tech sector (SMH, XLK) fell far harder than the rest of the market, while sectors like staples, health care, utilities, and financials actually held up better than the index. It reads as a severe but concentrated unwind in AI-adjacent names, not an undifferentiated panic.

“Why did gold fall during such a scary week? Isn't that backwards?” Usually gold rises on days like Friday, and last week a strong dollar explained why it wasn't — but Friday the dollar barely moved, so that explanation doesn't hold this time (Concept, above). The honest answer is we don't have a clean mechanism for it yet; worth flagging that uncertainty rather than reaching for a tidy story.
